40|BACKGROUND
41|The cyclooxygenase inhibitor ibuprofen may be used to treat patent ductus arteriosus
42|(PDA) in preterm infants. Whether selective early treatment of large PDAs with
43|ibuprofen would improve short-term outcomes is not known.
44|METHODS
45|We conducted a multicenter, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
46|evaluating early treatment (≤72 hours after birth) with ibuprofen for a large PDA
47|(diameter of ≥1.5 mm with pulsatile flow) in extremely preterm infants (born be-
48|tween 23 weeks 0 days' and 28 weeks 6 days' gestation). The primary outcome was a
49|composite of death or moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia evaluated at
50|36 weeks of postmenstrual age.
51|RESULTS
52|A total of 326 infants were assigned to receive ibuprofen and 327 to receive placebo;
53|324 and 322, respectively, had data available for outcome analyses. A primary-out-
54|come event occurred in 220 of 318 infants (69.2%) in the ibuprofen group and 202
55|of 318 infants (63.5%) in the placebo group (adjusted risk ratio, 1.09; 95% confi-
56|dence interval [CI], 0.98 to 1.20; P = 0.10). A total of 44 of 323 infants (13.6%) in
57|the ibuprofen group and 33 of 321 infants (10.3%) in the placebo group died
58|(adjusted risk ratio, 1.32; 95% CI, 0.92 to 1.90). Among the infants who survived
59|to 36 weeks of postmenstrual age, moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia
60|occurred in 176 of 274 (64.2%) in the ibuprofen group and 169 of 285 (59.3%) in
61|the placebo group (adjusted risk ratio, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.96 to 1.23). Two unforeseeable
62|serious adverse events occurred that were possibly related to ibuprofen.
63|CONCLUSIONS
64|The risk of death or moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dysplasia at 36 weeks
65|of postmenstrual age was not significantly lower among infants who received early
66|treatment with ibuprofen than among those who received placebo. (Funded by the
67|National Institute for Health Research Health Technology Assessment Pro-
68|gramme; Baby-OSCAR ISRCTN Registry number, ISRCTN84264977.)

3|Early Treatment of PDA with Ibuprofen
4|O
5|ver the past two decades, surviv-
6|al among extremely preterm infants has
7|increased alongside modest reductions
8|in neonatal morbidity, although the incidence of
9|bronchopulmonary dysplasia has increased.1 In
10|this gestation group, a large (≥1.5 mm in diam-
11|eter) patent ductus arteriosus (PDA) that is pres-
12|ent beyond 3 days of age is associated with higher
13|mortality and morbidity and a higher risk of
14|bronchopulmonary dysplasia than have been re-
15|ported among infants without a PDA.2 The inci-
16|dence of PDA is inversely proportional to gesta-
17|tional age at birth: more than 40% of infants born
18|at less than 28 weeks' gestation have persistent
19|PDA by 4 months of age.3,4 The risk of broncho-
20|pulmonary dysplasia or death in extremely pre-
21|term infants also increases with the persistence of
22|PDA beyond 1 to 2 weeks of age.5
23|Various treatment strategies have been inves-
24|tigated for the management of PDA.6 Prophylaxis
25|with indomethacin or ibuprofen in the first 12 to
26|24 hours of life has been reported to reduce the
27|risk of severe intraventricular hemorrhage and
28|pulmonary hemorrhage but has not been found
29|to increase survival without neurosensory impair-
30|ment at 18 months.7 However, if a prophylactic
31|approach is used, many infants will receive
32|treatment unnecessarily, since PDAs can close
33|spontaneously.8 Data on the treatment of infants
34|with a symptomatic PDA are limited, and reports
35|of improvements in clinical outcomes are lack-
36|ing.9 Consequently, the number of extremely pre-
37|term infants with a PDA who are treated pharma-
38|cologically has decreased.10
39|With the use of bedside functional echocar-
40|diography,11 infants can now be screened to iden-
41|tify large PDAs with unrestricted flow that are
42|unlikely to close spontaneously. Selective early
43|targeted treatment of patients with these PDAs
44|may make it possible to avoid unnecessary treat-
45|ment of all patients with PDAs.12 Parenteral indo-
46|methacin and ibuprofen have been used for early
47|targeted treatment of PDA, with no evidence of
48|a difference in their efficacy,13 although the side-
49|effect profile of ibuprofen has been reported to
50|be superior.6
51|We hypothesized that among patients with a
52|PDA of 1.5 mm or larger in diameter with unre-
53|stricted flow identified with the use of bedside
54|echocardiography, early selective treatment (≤72
55|hours after birth) with ibuprofen would reduce
56|mortality and improve short-term outcomes such
57|as bronchopulmonary dysplasia to a greater ex-
58|tent than placebo.
59|Methods
60|Trial Design
61|We conducted a multicenter, double-blind, ran-
62|domized, placebo-controlled trial in 32 neonatal
63|intensive care units in the United Kingdom in
64|accordance with a published protocol (available
65|with the full text of this article at NEJM.org).14
66|The main trial was preceded by an internal pilot
67|phase to assess the suitability of trial procedures
68|and recruitment. The clinicians, the infants' fami-
69|lies, and the persons who assessed outcomes
70|were unaware of the randomization assignments.14
71|The trial was coordinated by the National Perina-
72|tal Epidemiology Unit (NPEU) Clinical Trials Unit
73|at the University of Oxford, United Kingdom
74|(which was responsible for the conduct of the
75|trial), and was overseen by the trial steering com-
76|mittee, acting on the recommendations of an in-
77|dependent data and safety monitoring commit-
78|tee. The authors vouch for the accuracy and
79|completeness of the data and for the fidelity of
80|the trial to the protocol. Additional details are
81|provided in the Supplementary Appendix, avail-
82|able at NEJM.org.
83|Patients
84|After written informed consent was obtained
85|from the parents, infants born between 23 weeks
86|0 days' and 28 weeks 6 days' gestation who
87|were less than 72 hours old, were confirmed by
88|echocardiography to have a large PDA, and for
89|whom there were no associated clinical con-
90|cerns for acute pulmonary hypertension were
91|considered to be eligible for participation. A
92|large PDA was defined as a PDA with a diam-
93|eter of at least 1.5 mm and unrestricted trans-
94|ductal pulsatile (left-to-right shunting) flow. A
95|full list of the inclusion and exclusion criteria
96|is provided in Table S1 in the Supplementary
97|Appendix.
98|A Quick Take
99|is available at

4|Randomization
5|Dynamic randomization was performed with a
6|secure Web-based system that was created and
7|hosted by the NPEU Clinical Trials Unit with
8|24/7 telephone backup, ensuring concealment of
9|the group assignments. The randomization pro-
10|gram used a probabilistic minimization algorithm
11|and assigned patients in a 1:1 ratio to one of the
12|two groups to ensure balance with respect to the
13|size of the PDA, gestational age at birth, age, sex,
14|trial site, whether the infant was from a multiple
15|birth, mode of respiratory support, and whether
16|inotropes were received. Infants in multiple births
17|underwent randomization individually. Partici-
18|pants were enrolled by the delegated clinician at
19|the trial site.14
20|Intervention and Trial Procedures
21|The trial intervention was ibuprofen sodium,
22|and the matched placebo was a clear sterile solu-
23|tion of 0.9% sodium chloride. Each carton con-
24|taining ibuprofen or placebo was labeled with a
25|unique code in compliance with the guidance
26|provided in annex 13 of the European Commis-
27|sion guidelines for Good Manufacturing Prac-
28|tice. Ibuprofen was administered parenterally as
29|a loading dose of 10 mg per kilogram of body
30|weight, followed by two doses of 5 mg per kilo-
31|gram at least 24 hours apart. Placebo was ad-
32|ministered as an equal volume of 0.9% sodium
33|chloride (Table S2). Only one course of ibuprofen
34|or placebo was given. Prespecified criteria for
35|open-label medical or surgical treatment after
36|enrollment are shown in Table S3.
37|Transthoracic echocardiography was performed
38|to assess eligibility within 72 hours after birth
39|and at 3 weeks (18 to 24 days) of age to assess the
40|patency of the PDA while minimizing open-label
41|treatment. For quality control, a sample of echo-
42|cardiograms from 65 infants was reviewed inde-
43|pendently by a pediatric echocardiographer who
44|was unaware of the treatment assignments.
45|Outcomes
46|The primary outcome was a composite of death
47|or moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dyspla-
48|sia assessed at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age15
49|(Tables S4 and S5). A physiological challenge of
50|supplemental oxygen reduction was used to test
51|for oxygen need at 36 weeks of postmenstrual
52|age16 to differentiate mild from moderate bron-
53|chopulmonary dysplasia (Fig. S1). Secondary
54|short-term outcomes up to the time of discharge
55|included individual components of the primary
56|outcome, the severity of bronchopulmonary dys-
57|plasia, severe intraventricular hemorrhage, cystic
58|periventricular leukomalacia, retinopathy of pre-
59|maturity requiring treatment, clinically signifi-
60|cant pulmonary hemorrhage, acute pulmonary
61|hypertension, definitive necrotizing enterocoli-
62|tis, closed or clinically nonsignificant PDA less
63|than 1.5 mm in diameter with restricted flow at
64|3 weeks age, open-label treatment of a PDA caus-
65|ing symptoms, weight gain, and discharge home
66|while receiving supplemental oxygen (Table
67|S5).14 Other secondary short-term outcomes are
68|listed in the Supplementary Appendix and in the
69|statistical analysis plan (available with the pro-
70|tocol).17 All outcome data were recorded rou-
71|tinely, including demographic data and compli-
72|cations of prematurity; these data were obtained
73|from clinical notes or trial-related assessments
74|(Table S6).
75|A list of foreseeable serious adverse events
76|that are common in this patient population was
77|prespecified (see section 9.1.4 in the protocol);
78|unforeseeable serious adverse events were de-
79|fined as those that were not included on this
80|list. A serious adverse reaction was defined as a
81|serious adverse event that was considered to
82|have been caused by the administration of the
83|trial agent; if such an event was not consistent
84|with the safety profile of the trial agent, it was
85|classed as a suspected unexpected serious ad-
86|verse reaction.14
87|Statistical Analysis
88|The incidence of the primary outcome was pre-
89|dicted to be 60% in the placebo group (see Sup-
90|plementary Methods). A sample of 730 infants was
91|calculated to be required in order to detect a
92|clinically important absolute risk reduction of 12
93|percentage points (i.e., an incidence of 60% in
94|the placebo group and an incidence of 48% in the
95|ibuprofen group) with 90% power and a type I
96|error of 5% under the assumption that 1% of in-
97|fants would be lost to follow-up.14
98|Analyses were performed according to the
99|intention-to-treat principle, with infants exclud-
100|ed from the analysis only if their data were miss-

5|adjusted for minimization factors, such as the
6|size of the PDA at randomization, gestational age
7|at birth, age at randomization, sex, whether the
8|infant was from a multiple birth, mode of respi-
9|ratory support at randomization, whether ino
10|tropes were received at the time of randomization,
11|and trial site, as well as for the correlation be-
12|tween siblings from multiple births, when tech-
13|nically possible (Table S7). Trial site was treated
14|as a random effect in the models, and all other
15|factors were treated as fixed effects. Binary out-
16|comes were analyzed by means of mixed-effects
17|Poisson regression with a robust variance esti-
18|mator; risk ratios and 95% confidence intervals
19|are reported. The assumptions used in the mod-
20|els were assessed and found to be valid (Fig. S2).
21|Continuous outcomes were analyzed with the
22|use of linear regression models; mean differences
23|and 95% confidence intervals (after checking
24|model assumptions) are reported. Because of the
25|large number of short-term outcomes, reporting
26|of differences between the groups and associat-
27|ed 95% confidence intervals was restricted to a
28|prespecified short list (Table S5). No formal
29|method to adjust for multiplicity was used; the
30|widths of the confidence intervals have not been
31|adjusted for multiplicity, and inferences drawn
32|may not be reproducible and should not be used
33|to infer definitive treatment effects for secondary
34|outcomes. Full details of the statistical analysis
35|are provided in the statistical analysis plan.17 Ad-
36|ditional details are provided in the Supplementary
37|Appendix. Stata/SE, version 15 (StataCorp), was
38|used for all analyses.
39|Results
40|Patients
41|From July 2015 through December 2020, a total
42|of 653 infants underwent randomization: 326 were
43|assigned to receive ibuprofen and 327 to receive
44|placebo. A total of 22 infants underwent ran-
45|domization during the internal pilot phase and
46|631 during the main recruitment phase (Fig. 1).
47|Maternal and infant baseline characteristics ap-
48|peared to be well balanced between the groups
49|(Table 1 and Table S8). The median PDA diam-
50|eter was 2.2 mm (interquartile range, 1.9 to 2.6).
51|An independent audit of the echocardiograms
52|indicated that 93.8% of infants who underwent
53|randomization in the trial met the prespecified
54|echocardiographic eligibility criteria. The remain-
55|der of the echocardiographic images could not
56|be assessed accurately to confirm the eligibility
57|criteria.
58|A total 318 of 326 infants (97.5%) in the ibu-

67|Discussion
68|In this double-blind, randomized, placebo-con-
69|trolled trial involving extremely preterm infants
70|with a large PDA, we found no evidence that
71|early treatment with ibuprofen was associated with
72|a lower incidence of death or moderate or severe
73|bronchopulmonary dysplasia at 36 weeks of post-
74|menstrual age than placebo. There was no sig-
75|nificant between-group difference in either the
76|risk of death or the risk of moderate or severe
77|bronchopulmonary dysplasia.
78|Our results are broadly consistent with those
79|of other studies of early targeted treatment of
80|PDA with ibuprofen that have not shown a con-

15|Variation in the rate of PDA closure among stud-

20|nous ibuprofen administered within a standard
21|dosing regimen was chosen as the intervention
22|in our trial because higher doses are usually used
23|only when an infant is 7 days of age or older, and
24|it was the most common treatment schedule for
25|infants with a PDA in the United Kingdom at the
26|time the trial was designed.27 Similarly, most
27|units did not routinely repeat echocardiographic
28|assessment after ibuprofen therapy with the in-
29|tention of offering a second course if the PDA
30|remained patent.

32|atic PDA appeared to be less common in this
33|trial than in other, similar trials28 and occurred
34|almost twice as frequently in the placebo group

36|noninferiority trial of early ibuprofen treatment
37|in the management of PDA showed a very low
38|percentage of patients (0.7%) receiving open-label
39|medical therapy in the expectant management
40|group,19 there was frequent use of acetamino-

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

Randomization
Dynamic randomization was performed with a
secure Web-based system that was created and
hosted by the NPEU Clinical Trials Unit with
24/7 telephone backup, ensuring concealment of
the group assignments. The randomization pro-
gram used a probabilistic minimization algorithm
and assigned patients in a 1:1 ratio to one of the
two groups to ensure balance with respect to the
size of the PDA, gestational age at birth, age, sex,
trial site, whether the infant was from a multiple
birth, mode of respiratory support, and whether
inotropes were received. Infants in multiple births
underwent randomization individually. Partici-
pants were enrolled by the delegated clinician at
the trial site.14
Intervention and Trial Procedures
The trial intervention was ibuprofen sodium,
and the matched placebo was a clear sterile solu-
tion of 0.9% sodium chloride. Each carton con-
taining ibuprofen or placebo was labeled with a
unique code in compliance with the guidance
provided in annex 13 of the European Commis-
sion guidelines for Good Manufacturing Prac-
tice. Ibuprofen was administered parenterally as
a loading dose of 10 mg per kilogram of body
weight, followed by two doses of 5 mg per kilo-
gram at least 24 hours apart. Placebo was ad-
ministered as an equal volume of 0.9% sodium
chloride (Table S2). Only one course of ibuprofen
or placebo was given. Prespecified criteria for
open-label medical or surgical treatment after
enrollment are shown in Table S3.
Transthoracic echocardiography was performed
to assess eligibility within 72 hours after birth
and at 3 weeks (18 to 24 days) of age to assess the
patency of the PDA while minimizing open-label
treatment. For quality control, a sample of echo-
cardiograms from 65 infants was reviewed inde-
pendently by a pediatric echocardiographer who
was unaware of the treatment assignments.

The primary outcome was a composite of death
or moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dyspla-
sia assessed at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age15
(Tables S4 and S5). A physiological challenge of
supplemental oxygen reduction was used to test
for oxygen need at 36 weeks of postmenstrual
age16 to differentiate mild from moderate bron-
chopulmonary dysplasia (Fig. S1). Secondary
short-term outcomes up to the time of discharge
included individual components of the primary
outcome, the severity of bronchopulmonary dys-
plasia, severe intraventricular hemorrhage, cystic
periventricular leukomalacia, retinopathy of pre-
maturity requiring treatment, clinically signifi-
cant pulmonary hemorrhage, acute pulmonary
hypertension, definitive necrotizing enterocoli-
tis, closed or clinically nonsignificant PDA less
than 1.5 mm in diameter with restricted flow at
3 weeks age, open-label treatment of a PDA caus-
ing symptoms, weight gain, and discharge home
while receiving supplemental oxygen (Table
S5).14 Other secondary short-term outcomes are
listed in the Supplementary Appendix and in the
statistical analysis plan (available with the pro-
tocol).17 All outcome data were recorded rou-
tinely, including demographic data and compli-
cations of prematurity; these data were obtained
from clinical notes or trial-related assessments
(Table S6).

serious adverse event that was considered to

Randomization
Dynamic randomization was performed with a
secure Web-based system that was created and
hosted by the NPEU Clinical Trials Unit with
24/7 telephone backup, ensuring concealment of
the group assignments. The randomization pro-
gram used a probabilistic minimization algorithm
and assigned patients in a 1:1 ratio to one of the
two groups to ensure balance with respect to the
size of the PDA, gestational age at birth, age, sex,
trial site, whether the infant was from a multiple
birth, mode of respiratory support, and whether
inotropes were received. Infants in multiple births
underwent randomization individually. Partici-
pants were enrolled by the delegated clinician at
the trial site.14
Intervention and Trial Procedures
The trial intervention was ibuprofen sodium,
and the matched placebo was a clear sterile solu-
tion of 0.9% sodium chloride. Each carton con-
taining ibuprofen or placebo was labeled with a
unique code in compliance with the guidance
provided in annex 13 of the European Commis-
sion guidelines for Good Manufacturing Prac-
tice. Ibuprofen was administered parenterally as
a loading dose of 10 mg per kilogram of body
weight, followed by two doses of 5 mg per kilo-
gram at least 24 hours apart. Placebo was ad-
ministered as an equal volume of 0.9% sodium
chloride (Table S2). Only one course of ibuprofen
or placebo was given. Prespecified criteria for
open-label medical or surgical treatment after
enrollment are shown in Table S3.
Transthoracic echocardiography was performed
to assess eligibility within 72 hours after birth
and at 3 weeks (18 to 24 days) of age to assess the
patency of the PDA while minimizing open-label
treatment. For quality control, a sample of echo-
cardiograms from 65 infants was reviewed inde-
pendently by a pediatric echocardiographer who
was unaware of the treatment assignments.
Outcomes
The primary outcome was a composite of death
or moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dyspla-
sia assessed at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age15
(Tables S4 and S5). A physiological challenge of
supplemental oxygen reduction was used to test
for oxygen need at 36 weeks of postmenstrual
age16 to differentiate mild from moderate bron-
chopulmonary dysplasia (Fig. S1). Secondary
short-term outcomes up to the time of discharge
included individual components of the primary
outcome, the severity of bronchopulmonary dys-
plasia, severe intraventricular hemorrhage, cystic
periventricular leukomalacia, retinopathy of pre-
maturity requiring treatment, clinically signifi-
cant pulmonary hemorrhage, acute pulmonary
hypertension, definitive necrotizing enterocoli-
tis, closed or clinically nonsignificant PDA less
than 1.5 mm in diameter with restricted flow at
3 weeks age, open-label treatment of a PDA caus-
ing symptoms, weight gain, and discharge home
while receiving supplemental oxygen (Table
S5).14 Other secondary short-term outcomes are
listed in the Supplementary Appendix and in the
statistical analysis plan (available with the pro-
tocol).17 All outcome data were recorded rou-
tinely, including demographic data and compli-
cations of prematurity; these data were obtained
from clinical notes or trial-related assessments
(Table S6).
A list of foreseeable serious adverse events
that are common in this patient population was
prespecified (see section 9.1.4 in the protocol);
unforeseeable serious adverse events were de-
fined as those that were not included on this
list. A serious adverse reaction was defined as a
serious adverse event that was considered to
have been caused by the administration of the
trial agent; if such an event was not consistent
with the safety profile of the trial agent, it was
classed as a suspected unexpected serious ad-
verse reaction.14
Statistical Analysis
The incidence of the primary outcome was pre-
dicted to be 60% in the placebo group (see Sup-
plementary Methods). A sample of 730 infants was
calculated to be required in order to detect a
clinically important absolute risk reduction of 12
percentage points (i.e., an incidence of 60% in
the placebo group and an incidence of 48% in the
ibuprofen group) with 90% power and a type I
error of 5% under the assumption that 1% of in-
fants would be lost to follow-up.14

left_facts: The protocol prohibited rescue treatment. The treating clinician provided rescue because of the patient's symptoms, as the clinician would in ordinary care.
paired_examples.reasoning_focus: Hold protocol inconsistency, personnel and conduct fixed; distinguish ordinary care from an allocation-driven decision. Personnel identity alone supplies no cause.

right_facts: The same protocol required twelve exercise sessions. A participant stopped the same program because additional research-only appointments prevented attendance.

paired_examples.changed_premise: the source-stated exclusion rule and outcome availability

Randomization
Dynamic randomization was performed with a
secure Web-based system that was created and
hosted by the NPEU Clinical Trials Unit with
24/7 telephone backup, ensuring concealment of
the group assignments. The randomization pro-
gram used a probabilistic minimization algorithm
and assigned patients in a 1:1 ratio to one of the
two groups to ensure balance with respect to the
size of the PDA, gestational age at birth, age, sex,
trial site, whether the infant was from a multiple
birth, mode of respiratory support, and whether
inotropes were received. Infants in multiple births
underwent randomization individually. Partici-
pants were enrolled by the delegated clinician at
the trial site.14
Intervention and Trial Procedures
The trial intervention was ibuprofen sodium,
and the matched placebo was a clear sterile solu-
tion of 0.9% sodium chloride. Each carton con-
taining ibuprofen or placebo was labeled with a
unique code in compliance with the guidance
provided in annex 13 of the European Commis-
sion guidelines for Good Manufacturing Prac-
tice. Ibuprofen was administered parenterally as
a loading dose of 10 mg per kilogram of body
weight, followed by two doses of 5 mg per kilo-
gram at least 24 hours apart. Placebo was ad-
ministered as an equal volume of 0.9% sodium
chloride (Table S2). Only one course of ibuprofen
or placebo was given. Prespecified criteria for
open-label medical or surgical treatment after
enrollment are shown in Table S3.
Transthoracic echocardiography was performed
to assess eligibility within 72 hours after birth
and at 3 weeks (18 to 24 days) of age to assess the
patency of the PDA while minimizing open-label
treatment. For quality control, a sample of echo-
cardiograms from 65 infants was reviewed inde-
pendently by a pediatric echocardiographer who
was unaware of the treatment assignments.

The primary outcome was a composite of death
or moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dyspla-
sia assessed at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age15
(Tables S4 and S5). A physiological challenge of
supplemental oxygen reduction was used to test
for oxygen need at 36 weeks of postmenstrual
age16 to differentiate mild from moderate bron-
chopulmonary dysplasia (Fig. S1). Secondary
short-term outcomes up to the time of discharge
included individual components of the primary
outcome, the severity of bronchopulmonary dys-
plasia, severe intraventricular hemorrhage, cystic
periventricular leukomalacia, retinopathy of pre-
maturity requiring treatment, clinically signifi-
cant pulmonary hemorrhage, acute pulmonary
hypertension, definitive necrotizing enterocoli-
tis, closed or clinically nonsignificant PDA less
than 1.5 mm in diameter with restricted flow at
3 weeks age, open-label treatment of a PDA caus-
ing symptoms, weight gain, and discharge home
while receiving supplemental oxygen (Table
S5).14 Other secondary short-term outcomes are
listed in the Supplementary Appendix and in the
statistical analysis plan (available with the pro-
tocol).17 All outcome data were recorded rou-
tinely, including demographic data and compli-
cations of prematurity; these data were obtained
from clinical notes or trial-related assessments
(Table S6).

serious adverse event that was considered to
have been caused by the administration of the
trial agent; if such an event was not consistent

response_framework.firm_evidence_rule: The definitive versions (‘Yes’ and ‘No’) would typically imply that firm evidence is available in relation to the signalling question.
response_framework.probable_judgment_rule: The ‘Probably’ versions would typically imply that a judgement has been made. ‘Yes’ and ‘Probably yes’ have the same implications for risk of bias, as do ‘No’ and ‘Probably no’.
response_framework.no_information_rule: Use ‘No information’ only when both (i) insufficient details are reported to permit a response of ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’, and (ii) in the absence of these details it would be unreasonable to respond ‘Probably yes’ or ‘Probably no’ in the circumstances of the trial.
response_framework.independence_rule: Signalling questions should be answered independently: the answer to one question should not affect answers to other questions in the same or other domains other than through determining which subsequent questions are answered.
response_framework.quotation_rule: Brief direct quotations from the text of the study report should be used whenever possible to support the answer.

considerations: Compare actual methods and detection opportunities. Assessor awareness or possible reporting influence alone does not establish a between-group method difference; assess awareness and influence in 4.3 to 4.5.

Detection opportunity is the chance an outcome could be identified or recorded, including passive ascertainment or intervention-related visits. Keep it separate from measurement susceptibility (4.1) and from who knew the assignment (4.3).
A different visit schedule or passive collection is not enough on its own: explain how it could make the approved outcome more or less likely to be detected in one group.

Tie every monitoring difference to the approved event. Extra visits for toxicity monitoring do not establish differential measurement of mortality when death is captured through the same complete registry in both groups; those same visits may change detection of a lab-detected toxicity measured at those visits. State any mortality-specific pathway if one is supported.

For adverse events, compare the actual start and end of the AE observation window, visit schedule, post-treatment follow-up, and ascertainment method with the approved safety window. Treatment duration, median progression-free survival, or a treatment-emergent label alone does not establish when or how adverse events were observed.
Neutral paired control: equal ascertainment schedules and intervention-created additional visits differ only in detection opportunity; do not turn that contrast into an automatic risk label.

Randomization
Dynamic randomization was performed with a
secure Web-based system that was created and
hosted by the NPEU Clinical Trials Unit with
24/7 telephone backup, ensuring concealment of
the group assignments. The randomization pro-
gram used a probabilistic minimization algorithm
and assigned patients in a 1:1 ratio to one of the
two groups to ensure balance with respect to the
size of the PDA, gestational age at birth, age, sex,
trial site, whether the infant was from a multiple
birth, mode of respiratory support, and whether
inotropes were received. Infants in multiple births
underwent randomization individually. Partici-
pants were enrolled by the delegated clinician at
the trial site.14
Intervention and Trial Procedures
The trial intervention was ibuprofen sodium,
and the matched placebo was a clear sterile solu-
tion of 0.9% sodium chloride. Each carton con-
taining ibuprofen or placebo was labeled with a
unique code in compliance with the guidance
provided in annex 13 of the European Commis-
sion guidelines for Good Manufacturing Prac-
tice. Ibuprofen was administered parenterally as
a loading dose of 10 mg per kilogram of body
weight, followed by two doses of 5 mg per kilo-
gram at least 24 hours apart. Placebo was ad-
ministered as an equal volume of 0.9% sodium
chloride (Table S2). Only one course of ibuprofen
or placebo was given. Prespecified criteria for
open-label medical or surgical treatment after
enrollment are shown in Table S3.
Transthoracic echocardiography was performed
to assess eligibility within 72 hours after birth
and at 3 weeks (18 to 24 days) of age to assess the
patency of the PDA while minimizing open-label
treatment. For quality control, a sample of echo-
cardiograms from 65 infants was reviewed inde-
pendently by a pediatric echocardiographer who
was unaware of the treatment assignments.
Outcomes
The primary outcome was a composite of death
or moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dyspla-
sia assessed at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age15
(Tables S4 and S5). A physiological challenge of
supplemental oxygen reduction was used to test
for oxygen need at 36 weeks of postmenstrual
age16 to differentiate mild from moderate bron-
chopulmonary dysplasia (Fig. S1). Secondary
short-term outcomes up to the time of discharge
included individual components of the primary
outcome, the severity of bronchopulmonary dys-
plasia, severe intraventricular hemorrhage, cystic
periventricular leukomalacia, retinopathy of pre-
maturity requiring treatment, clinically signifi-
cant pulmonary hemorrhage, acute pulmonary
hypertension, definitive necrotizing enterocoli-
tis, closed or clinically nonsignificant PDA less
than 1.5 mm in diameter with restricted flow at
3 weeks age, open-label treatment of a PDA caus-
ing symptoms, weight gain, and discharge home
while receiving supplemental oxygen (Table
S5).14 Other secondary short-term outcomes are
listed in the Supplementary Appendix and in the
statistical analysis plan (available with the pro-
tocol).17 All outcome data were recorded rou-
tinely, including demographic data and compli-
cations of prematurity; these data were obtained
from clinical notes or trial-related assessments
(Table S6).
A list of foreseeable serious adverse events
that are common in this patient population was
prespecified (see section 9.1.4 in the protocol);
unforeseeable serious adverse events were de-
fined as those that were not included on this
list. A serious adverse reaction was defined as a
serious adverse event that was considered to
have been caused by the administration of the
trial agent; if such an event was not consistent
with the safety profile of the trial agent, it was
classed as a suspected unexpected serious ad-
verse reaction.14
Statistical Analysis
The incidence of the primary outcome was pre-
dicted to be 60% in the placebo group (see Sup-
plementary Methods). A sample of 730 infants was
calculated to be required in order to detect a
clinically important absolute risk reduction of 12

the placebo group and an incidence of 48% in the
ibuprofen group) with 90% power and a type I
error of 5% under the assumption that 1% of in-
fants would be lost to follow-up.14

Randomization
Dynamic randomization was performed with a
secure Web-based system that was created and
hosted by the NPEU Clinical Trials Unit with
24/7 telephone backup, ensuring concealment of
the group assignments. The randomization pro-
gram used a probabilistic minimization algorithm
and assigned patients in a 1:1 ratio to one of the
two groups to ensure balance with respect to the
size of the PDA, gestational age at birth, age, sex,
trial site, whether the infant was from a multiple
birth, mode of respiratory support, and whether
inotropes were received. Infants in multiple births
underwent randomization individually. Partici-
pants were enrolled by the delegated clinician at
the trial site.14
Intervention and Trial Procedures
The trial intervention was ibuprofen sodium,
and the matched placebo was a clear sterile solu-
tion of 0.9% sodium chloride. Each carton con-
taining ibuprofen or placebo was labeled with a
unique code in compliance with the guidance
provided in annex 13 of the European Commis-
sion guidelines for Good Manufacturing Prac-
tice. Ibuprofen was administered parenterally as
a loading dose of 10 mg per kilogram of body
weight, followed by two doses of 5 mg per kilo-
gram at least 24 hours apart. Placebo was ad-
ministered as an equal volume of 0.9% sodium
chloride (Table S2). Only one course of ibuprofen
or placebo was given. Prespecified criteria for
open-label medical or surgical treatment after
enrollment are shown in Table S3.
Transthoracic echocardiography was performed
to assess eligibility within 72 hours after birth
and at 3 weeks (18 to 24 days) of age to assess the
patency of the PDA while minimizing open-label
treatment. For quality control, a sample of echo-
cardiograms from 65 infants was reviewed inde-
pendently by a pediatric echocardiographer who
was unaware of the treatment assignments.
Outcomes
The primary outcome was a composite of death
or moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dyspla-
sia assessed at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age15
(Tables S4 and S5). A physiological challenge of
supplemental oxygen reduction was used to test
for oxygen need at 36 weeks of postmenstrual
age16 to differentiate mild from moderate bron-
chopulmonary dysplasia (Fig. S1). Secondary
short-term outcomes up to the time of discharge
included individual components of the primary
outcome, the severity of bronchopulmonary dys-
plasia, severe intraventricular hemorrhage, cystic
periventricular leukomalacia, retinopathy of pre-
maturity requiring treatment, clinically signifi-
cant pulmonary hemorrhage, acute pulmonary
hypertension, definitive necrotizing enterocoli-
tis, closed or clinically nonsignificant PDA less
than 1.5 mm in diameter with restricted flow at
3 weeks age, open-label treatment of a PDA caus-
ing symptoms, weight gain, and discharge home
while receiving supplemental oxygen (Table
S5).14 Other secondary short-term outcomes are
listed in the Supplementary Appendix and in the
statistical analysis plan (available with the pro-
tocol).17 All outcome data were recorded rou-
tinely, including demographic data and compli-
cations of prematurity; these data were obtained
from clinical notes or trial-related assessments
(Table S6).
A list of foreseeable serious adverse events
that are common in this patient population was
prespecified (see section 9.1.4 in the protocol);
unforeseeable serious adverse events were de-
fined as those that were not included on this
list. A serious adverse reaction was defined as a
serious adverse event that was considered to
have been caused by the administration of the
trial agent; if such an event was not consistent
with the safety profile of the trial agent, it was
classed as a suspected unexpected serious ad-
verse reaction.14
Statistical Analysis
The incidence of the primary outcome was pre-
dicted to be 60% in the placebo group (see Sup-
plementary Methods). A sample of 730 infants was
calculated to be required in order to detect a
clinically important absolute risk reduction of 12

ibuprofen group) with 90% power and a type I
error of 5% under the assumption that 1% of in-

7|2.9
8|Intervention allocation
9|Treatment allocation of ibuprofen or placebo will be in a ratio of 1:1 and masked such that
10|the allocation will not be known by clinicians, the baby's family or the trial outcome
11|assessors.
12|
13|Randomisation will be managed via a secure web-based randomisation facility hosted by the
14|NPEU CTU with telephone back-up available at all times (24/7, 365 days a year). The
15|randomisation program will use a minimisation algorithm to ensure balance between the
16|groups with respect to the size of the PDA (1.5 mm to < 2.0 mm; 2.0 mm to < 3.0 mm; ≥ 3.0
17|mm), gestational age at birth (23 to 23+6 weeks; 24 to 24+6 weeks; 25 to 25+6 weeks; 26 to
18|26+6 weeks; 27 to 27+6 weeks; 28 to 28+6 weeks), age at randomisation (< 12 hours; 12 to <
19|24 hours; 24 to < 48 hours; 48 to < 72 hours), sex (male; female or indeterminate), trial site,
20|multiple births, mode of respiratory support at randomisation ((1) invasive ventilation (by an
21|endotracheal tube); or (2) non-invasive respiratory support through, nasal CPAP, nasal
22|ventilation, humidified high flow nasal cannula therapy or, low flow oxygen ≥ 1.1L/min; or
23|(3) receiving no mechanical ventilation, or pressure support (in room air, or low flow oxygen
24|<1.1 L/min, or ambient oxygen)), and receiving inotropes or not at the time of
25|randomisation. Babies of multiple births will be randomised individually.
26|
27|The Senior Trials Programmer at the NPEU CTU will write the randomisation program and
28|hold the treatment allocation codes. If necessary, the code may be broken for a single baby
29|at the request of the site PI or clinician in charge of the baby.
30|
31|2.10 Data collection schedule
32|Data will be collected using paper case report forms (CRFs) at the centres and entered into
33|the study's OpenClinica electronic database by NPEU CTU staff.
34|
35|The CRFs to be completed are as follows:
36| Form 1: Trial entry
37| Form 2: Trial medication
38| Form 3: ECHO results
39| Form 4: 36-week form
40| Form 5: Open label treatment of PDA
41| Form 6: Baby outcomes
42| Form 6a: Necrotising enterocolitis report form
43| Form 7: Baby withdrawal form
44| Form 8a: SAE report form
45| Form 8b: SAE assessment form
46| Form 8c: SAE processing form
47| Form 9a: Incident and deviation form
48| Form 9b: Incident deviation and serious breach form
49|
50|Additionally, a two-year follow-up questionnaire will be sent to parents of participating
51|infants when they reach 2 years of age. These will be completed by the parents, either on
52|the paper questionnaire or an online form, followed by data entry into the study's
53|OpenClinica database by NPEU CTU staff, where necessary.

32|Protocol non-compliances
33|A protocol non-compliance is defined as a failure to adhere to the protocol such as the
34|wrong intervention being administered, incorrect data being collected and documented,
35|errors in applying inclusion/exclusion criteria or missed follow-up visits due to error.
36|
37|All protocol non-compliances will be listed in the final report. Non-compliances are defined
38|below.
39|
40|3.1
41|Major
42|The following are pre-defined major protocol non-compliances with a direct bearing on the
43|primary outcome:
44| Data considered to be fraudulent

47|Minor
48|The following will be defined as minor protocol non-compliances:
49|
50|Participants randomised in error
51|These include infants:
52| who are < 23 weeks or ≥ 29 weeks of gestation
53| who are ≥ 72 hours old
54| with a PDA < 1.5 mm in diameter OR who does not have unrestrictive pulsatile left to
55|right flow or, growing pattern with right to left flow of 30% or more

8| where written informed consent has not been obtained from the parent(s)
9| with a severe congenital anomaly
10| with contraindications to the use of ibuprofen
11| who have had indomethacin, ibuprofen, or paracetamol administered after birth.

13|Treatment non-compliances
14|These include infants who:
15| do not receive allocated intervention. These include infants who were allocated
16|ibuprofen, who instead received placebo, and vice versa.
17| do not receive the correct number of doses. These include infants who received less
18|than 3 doses of the trial medication.
19| do not receive medication at the correct time. These include infants who received
20|their first dose later than 72 hours after birth, or received their 2nd or 3rd dose
21|outside the specified dosing window (< 18 hours or > 72 hours between doses 1 and
22|2, or doses 2 and 3; or dose 3 completed > 7 days after first dose administered).
23| received open-label treatment without meeting the criteria. These include infants
24|who received open-label treatment but did not meet the defined criteria for doing
25|so:
26|1. Inability to wean on ventilator (ventilated for at least 7 days continuously)
27|and any of: inability to wean oxygen; persistent hypotension; pulmonary
28|haemorrhage; signs of cardiac failure,
29|AND
30|2. Echocardiographic findings of a large PDA (PDA ≥ 2.0 mm with pulsatile
31|flow)
32|AND
33|3. Echocardiographic findings of hyperdynamic circulation or ductal steal.
34|
35|Trial procedure non-compliances:
36| ECHO not done around 3 weeks (18-24 days) of age
37| Oxygen reduction test not done when baby was eligible

8|INTRODUCTION
9|
10|This document details the proposed presentation and analyses for the main analysis
11|reporting the short-term results from the National Institute for Health Research (NIHR)
12|Health Technology Assessment (HTA) programme funded multi-centre, masked, randomised
13|controlled trial, Baby-OSCAR.
14|
15|The results reported will follow the strategy set out here, which adheres to the guidelines
16|for the content of a statistical analysis plan (SAP). Subsequent analyses of a more
17|exploratory nature will not be bound by this strategy, though they are expected to follow

19|analysis (e.g. to decide cut-points for categorisation of continuous variables), nor to prohibit
20|accepted practices (e.g. data transformation prior to analysis), but they are intended to
21|establish the rules that will be followed, as closely as possible, when analysing and reporting
22|the trial.

8|BACKGROUND INFORMATION
9|
10|2.1
11|Rationale
12|Baby-OSCAR is a masked, multi-centre randomised placebo-controlled parallel group trial to
13|determine short- and long-term health and economic outcomes of the treatment of a large
14|Patent Ductus Arteriosus (PDA) in extremely preterm babies with ibuprofen within 72 hours
15|of birth.
16|
17|The main trial follows an internal pilot phase, which has been run to assess the suitability of
18|trial procedures and likelihood of recruitment targets being achieved. The trial aimed to
19|recruit approximately 730 infants in total (including those recruited during the internal pilot
20|phase) from 35 UK tertiary neonatal units (and 5 for the internal pilot phase).
21|
22|PDA is associated with a number of serious and life-threatening short and long term
23|complications including low blood pressure (hypotension), bleeding in the lungs (pulmonary
24|haemorrhage) and brain (intraventricular haemorrhage (IVH)), systemic complications such
25|as necrotising enterocolitis (NEC), bronchopulmonary dysplasia (BPD), and long term health
26|problems such as neurodevelopmental disability and chronic respiratory problems. The
27|persistence of PDA is associated with an 8-fold rise in neonatal mortality [Noori S et al,
28|2009]. In addition, as PDA is very common in extreme preterm babies and is associated with
29|a prolonged need for respiratory support and hospitalisation, it places a significant financial
30|burden on the National Health Service (NHS).
31|
32|Historically, clinicians who have been concerned about the complications associated with a
33|PDA have attempted to close PDAs utilising medical (pharmacological) or surgical treatment.
34|Traditionally, medical treatment is instituted as prophylactic treatment (within 24 hours of
35|birth) or symptomatic treatment (usually 5-7 days after birth). Prophylactic pharmacological
36|treatment of all preterm babies unnecessarily exposes a large proportion of babies to the
37|potentially serious side effects of drug treatment, when their PDA would have closed
38|spontaneously. Symptomatic treatment on the contrary delays treatment while waiting for
39|symptoms to appear and could result in a loss of treatment benefit as irreversible damage
40|may have already been done.
41|
42|Moreover, the practice of a conservative approach of not treating, seems to originate from
43|uncertainty regarding the management of PDA rather than evidence favouring no
44|intervention. This is because most studies conducted to date have involved more mature
45|preterm babies (over 1,000 g or 28 weeks of gestation) whose PDA is more likely to close
46|spontaneously. The studies were also largely designed to assess PDA closure rates rather
47|than clinically important outcomes.
48|
49|It is now suggested that large PDAs (those with a diameter of ≥1.5 mm) through which blood
50|flow is pulsatile and unrestricted are less likely to close spontaneously. Targeted early
51|treatment of large PDAs whilst asymptomatic has the potential to overcome the
52|disadvantages of both the prophylactic and symptomatic approaches. Although clinical
53|detection of PDA whilst asymptomatic is challenging, it can be assessed using bedside
54|echocardiography.
55|

7|Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs, especially indomethacin and ibuprofen have been
8|widely used for the treatment of PDA. Short term efficacy of indomethacin and ibuprofen
9|are equivalent in the treatment of PDA [Su BH et al, 2008]. Ibuprofen however appears to
10|reduce the risk of NEC and is associated with fewer clinical gastrointestinal and renal side
11|effects compared to indomethacin; hence it is the drug of choice for this trial. Paracetamol
12|has also been recently reported in case studies for closure of symptomatic PDA but further
13|research needs to be done to establish its effectiveness [Oncel MY et al, 2013].
14|
15|The aim of this trial is to examine whether the pharmacological closure of a large PDA
16|(identified by echocardiography) in extremely preterm babies whilst asymptomatic has a
17|clinically important impact on both short- and long-term health and economic outcomes.
18|
19|
20|2.2
21|Objectives of the trial
22|
23|2.2.1 Primary objective
24|To determine if selective early treatment of large PDAs (confirmed by echocardiograph) in
25|extremely preterm babies with ibuprofen within 72 hours of birth reduces the incidence of
26|death by 36 weeks of postmenstrual age or moderate or severe bronchopulmonary
27|dysplasia (BPD) at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age.
28|
29|2.2.2 Secondary objectives
30|To determine if the selective treatment of confirmed large PDAs in extremely preterm
31|babies with ibuprofen within 72 hours of birth results in:
32|
33| A reduction in the components of the primary outcome: death by 36 weeks of
34|postmenstrual age; moderate or severe BPD at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age,
35|severity of BPD at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age; other secondary outcomes up to
36|discharge (see Secondary Outcomes, section 2.6.2);
37|
38| Improved health outcomes at 2 years corrected age including survival without
39|moderate or severe neurodevelopmental disability (long-term primary objective)
40|and survival without respiratory morbidity (long-term secondary objective).
41|
42|An economic evaluation will be carried out from the perspective of the health service. It will
43|take the form of a cost-effectiveness analysis presented in terms of cost per major outcome
44|averted. The major outcomes are those of the primary outcome, namely death and
45|moderate or severe BPD by 36 weeks of postmenstrual age. Additional analyses will take
46|place on a range of secondary outcomes and on neurodevelopmental outcomes at 2 years.
47|The incremental cost estimate for statistically significant differences in the pre-specified
48|outcomes in primary and subgroup analyses would be computed.

12|Sample size & power
13|Evidence from the TIPP trial suggests that the risk of death or BPD in extremely low birth
14|weight babies at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age allocated placebo is 52% (95% CI 48% to
15|56%) [Schmidt et al, 2001]. However, this trial investigated the effect of prophylactic
16|treatment and included all babies weighing 500-999g. More recent information using data
17|derived from the latest report of Neonatal Survey Database from the Trent region (2010)
18|provides an approximate rate of death or BPD by 36 weeks of postmenstrual age of 53% for
19|all babies admitted to the neonatal unit. These babies would have been treated according to
20|clinical judgement and therefore a proportion of them would have been treated with
21|ibuprofen. Given that the risk of death or BPD in babies with a large PDA is inherently
22|higher, it is estimated that the risk in this group is 60%.
23|
24|Su et al (2008) compared ibuprofen to indomethacin in babies of ≤ 28 weeks of gestation
25|having a PDA who were less than 24 hours old. The combined outcome of death within 30
26|days or BPD at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age was observed to be 42% (95% CI 29% to
27|55%).
28|
29|It is therefore expected, given that babies will be enrolled up to 72 hours after birth, that
30|the treatment group incidence of death/BPD at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age will be
31|approximately 48% in the intervention arm. This would imply an absolute risk reduction of
32|12% (60% to 48%) in the primary outcome of the trial for babies randomised to treatment
33|compared to placebo, which is considered a clinically important difference.
34|
35|Some babies will require open-label treatment in either the treatment or placebo arm. As
36|open-label treatment should be limited to symptomatic babies meeting only defined
37|criteria, it is considered to have minimal or no effect on the primary outcome. Thus,
38|adjustment of the sample size for open-label treatment is not considered necessary.
